text: The previous lesson showed that non-adjacent qubits need SWAP gates to interact at all. This lesson goes one level deeper: what a SWAP actually costs in real gates, how compilers try to minimize that cost across a whole circuit, and why routing overhead can end up dominating the total error budget.

A SWAP gate exchanges the quantum states held by two qubits — whatever qubit A was holding, qubit B now holds, and vice versa. It's how a compiler physically relocates information: instead of teleporting a state to where it's needed, it walks it there one adjacent hop at a time. SWAP isn't a gate most hardware implements natively. On superconducting chips, it's standard to build one out of three CNOT gates in sequence, which together exchange the two qubits' states. Every SWAP a compiler inserts isn't one extra gate — it's three extra two-qubit gates, each with its own real error rate and execution time.

Here's how that compounds on a larger circuit. Take a circuit that would need 40 native two-qubit gates with perfect connectivity, but whose actual mapping onto a real device requires inserting 20 SWAPs — a realistic number for several long-range interactions on a sparse chip. Those 20 SWAPs cost 60 CNOT-equivalents, on top of the original 40, for 100 total two-qubit operations. At a representative 0.5 percent per-gate error rate, the 40-gate circuit alone carries roughly an 18 percent chance of at least one error; with the SWAP-derived gates added in, that climbs to roughly 39 percent — more than double, with routing overhead alone now responsible for more than half the circuit's total error risk.

For any circuit with more than a couple of two-qubit gates, a compiler is solving a real optimization problem: given the circuit's required interactions and the device's connectivity graph, find an assignment of logical to physical qubits, and a sequence of SWAPs, that inserts as few total SWAPs as possible. That inserted sequence is called a SWAP network. Real compilers use heuristic routing algorithms, because finding the provably optimal network is computationally expensive for anything but small circuits — good enough, fast enough is the practical standard. This is why routing and SWAP-network minimization get serious engineering attention: the same logical algorithm, compiled well versus poorly for a device's connectivity, can differ by a large margin in total error and runtime, without the algorithm itself changing at all.

Next lesson is this chapter's applied version: how to actually read a real published device connectivity map — the kind every provider console shows you — and use it to make a real decision about which physical qubits to run a circuit on.
